prompt: In the section's simple one-dimensional model of adsorption, E = E(d). What is the energy of the system a function of?

choices.text: Only the distance d from the surface
The distance d and the molecule's orientation
choices.why: The angular orientation is one of the parameters the model neglects. Its one variable is the distance d of the molecule from the surface.

choices.text: The distance d and its position along the surface
choices.why: The position parallel to the surface plane is neglected too. The 1D model keeps only the distance d from the surface.

choices.text: How much of the surface is already covered
choices.why: Coverage does affect adsorption, but the model first sets it aside. In E = E(d), the only variable is the distance d.

explanation: The model follows a single molecule as it approaches the surface, so its energy depends only on d. The section stresses that this is very simplistic: it neglects the molecule's orientation, changes in its bond lengths and angles, and its position parallel to the surface.

prompt: Which situation does the section first describe with its simple 1D potential energy curve?

choices.text: An isolated molecule meeting a clean surface
A molecule meeting a partly covered surface
choices.why: Pre-adsorbed molecules change the interaction; that is the effect of surface coverage, which the section sets aside at first. It starts with a clean surface.

choices.text: A molecule meeting a surface with impurities
choices.why: The section names impurities as adsorbed species that change the interaction. The simple model starts with an isolated molecule and a clean surface.

choices.text: A molecule moving across the surface plane
choices.why: The position parallel to the surface is one of the parameters the model neglects. It follows the molecule only as d, its distance from the surface, changes.

explanation: The interaction of a molecule with a surface depends on any species already adsorbed there, whether impurities or molecules of the same kind. The section nevertheless starts with an isolated molecule and a clean surface, using the 1D model E = E(d).

prompt: According to the section, what differentiates physisorption from chemisorption?

choices.text: The strength of the interaction with the surface
Whether the particle is an atom or a molecule
choices.why: The section pictures both atoms and molecules physisorbed and chemisorbed. The two types differ in how strongly the particle interacts with the surface.

choices.text: The orientation of the adsorbed molecule
choices.why: The figures note that molecules can adsorb at various orientations in both cases. The difference is the strength of the interaction.

choices.text: Whether the surface is a metal or not
choices.why: The section's example of pure physisorption is Ar on metals, so a metal surface can physisorb. The two types differ in interaction strength.

explanation: The section distinguishes the two by the strength of interaction between the adsorbed particle and the surface. Physisorption comes from weak van der Waals forces; chemisorption involves forming a chemical bond with the surface.

prompt: The same atom can either physisorb or chemisorb on a surface, sitting on average a distance d_ph or d_ch from it. How do the two distances compare?

choices.text: d_ph is always greater than d_ch
d_ch is always greater than d_ph
choices.why: The order is reversed. A chemisorbed atom is bonded to the surface and sits closer; the physisorbed one is held farther out by weak forces.

choices.text: They are equal; only the energy differs
choices.why: The two minima sit at different distances. The physisorption minimum lies farther out, so d_ph > d_ch.

choices.text: It depends on whether it is an atom or a molecule
choices.why: The section shows d_ph > d_ch for atoms and for molecules alike. A physisorbed particle is always farther from the surface.

explanation: The section states that a physisorbed particle is always farther from the surface than an identical chemisorbed one. On the potential energy curve, the shallow physisorption minimum lies at larger d than the deep chemisorption minimum.

prompt: In pure physisorption, such as Ar on metals, what is the only attraction between the adsorbing species and the surface?

choices.text: Weak van der Waals forces
Strong van der Waals forces
choices.why: The section calls these forces weak, which is why the physisorption well is shallow. Strong binding comes from chemical bonds.

choices.text: Chemical bonds with surface atoms
choices.why: Bond formation with the surface is chemisorption. In pure physisorption the only attraction is weak van der Waals forces.

choices.text: The overlap of electron density
choices.why: Electron density overlap gives strong repulsion, the steep rise in energy close to the surface. The attraction comes from van der Waals forces.

explanation: In pure physisorption, no chemical bond forms; the only attraction is from weak van der Waals forces. These give a shallow minimum in the potential energy curve, before repulsion from electron density overlap takes over at short distances.

prompt: Where does the section place the physisorption minimum on the potential energy curve?

choices.text: A shallow well at large d, typically d > 0.3 nm
A deep well at large d, typically d > 0.3 nm
choices.why: The distance is right, but the well is shallow: van der Waals forces are weak. The deep well belongs to chemisorption.

choices.text: A shallow well right at the surface, d near 0
choices.why: Very close to the surface, repulsion from electron density overlap makes the energy rise sharply. The physisorption minimum lies relatively far out.

choices.text: A deep well at short d, close to the surface
choices.why: That describes the chemisorption well. Physisorption gives a shallow minimum at a relatively large distance.

explanation: Weak van der Waals forces give a shallow minimum at a relatively large distance from the surface, typically more than 0.3 nm. Closer in, strong repulsion from electron density overlap makes the total energy rise rapidly.

prompt: If a physisorbed atom is pushed closer to the surface than d_ph, its energy rises rapidly. What does the section say causes this?

choices.text: Repulsion from overlapping electron density
Loss of the van der Waals attraction
choices.why: Losing a weak attraction could only raise the energy a little. The steep rise comes from strong repulsive forces as the electron densities overlap.

choices.text: The cost of forming chemical bonds
choices.why: Forming chemical bonds lowers the energy; that is the chemisorption well. The steep rise is repulsion from electron density overlap.

choices.text: An activation barrier to physisorption
choices.why: Physisorption has no barrier, and this rise lies inside the well, not before it. It is the repulsion of overlapping electron densities.

explanation: The van der Waals attraction gives the shallow well at d_ph. Closer than that, strong repulsive forces from electron density overlap make the total energy climb steeply, which sets the inner wall of the well.

prompt: Why does the section say the kinetics of physisorption are invariably fast?

choices.text: No barrier stands before the physisorption well
The physisorption well is very deep
choices.why: The physisorption well is shallow. Physisorption is fast because nothing blocks the way into the well: it is not activated.

choices.text: The barrier to physisorption is small
choices.why: There is no barrier at all. The process is not activated, so molecules enter the well freely.

choices.text: Molecules chemisorb first and then physisorb
choices.why: The order is reversed, and pure physisorption, like Ar on metals, has no chemisorption step. It is fast because it has no barrier.

explanation: Nothing prevents an approaching atom or molecule from entering the physisorption well, so the process is not activated. With no activation energy to overcome, physisorption is invariably fast.

prompt: An adsorbate can form chemical bonds with a surface. What does the section say happens to the weak physisorption attraction in such a system?

choices.text: It is still there, with a deeper chemisorption well closer in
It disappears, replaced by the chemisorption well
choices.why: The section says the weak, long-range physisorption forces are present to varying degrees in all adsorbate/substrate systems.

choices.text: It becomes the deeper of the two wells
choices.why: The physisorption well stays shallow. The PE curve is dominated by the much deeper chemisorption minimum.

choices.text: Its well moves closer in than the chemisorption well
choices.why: The physisorption well stays farther out: d_ph is greater than d_ch. The chemisorption minimum lies at shorter d.

explanation: Weak physisorption forces and their long-range attraction are present in all adsorbate/substrate systems. Where bonds can also form, the curve is dominated by a much deeper chemisorption minimum at shorter d.

prompt: For a molecule that can chemisorb, the real potential energy curve combines the physisorption and chemisorption curves, which cross at one point. What does the crossing mark as the molecule moves in?

choices.text: Chemisorption forces take over from physisorption
Physisorption forces take over from chemisorption
choices.why: It is the other way round. Far out, physisorption dominates; moving in past the crossing, chemisorption forces dominate.

choices.text: The energy reaches its overall minimum
choices.why: The overall minimum is the bottom of the chemisorption well, at d_ch. The crossing lies farther out, where chemisorption begins to dominate.

choices.text: The molecule desorbs into the gas phase
choices.why: The crossing is a point on the way in, not a desorption step. There, chemisorption forces begin to dominate over physisorption.

explanation: The minimum energy pathway follows the physisorption curve far from the surface and the chemisorption curve close to it. The curves cross where chemisorption forces begin to dominate over physisorption alone, and the combined curve differs most from the separate ones near that point.

prompt: On the overall potential energy curve for chemisorption, what does the depth of the chemisorption well represent?

choices.text: The energy of adsorption, ΔE(ads)
The equilibrium bond distance, d_ch
choices.why: d_ch is where the minimum lies along the horizontal axis. Its depth, on the energy axis, is the energy of adsorption.

choices.text: The depth of the physisorption well
choices.why: The physisorption well is a separate, shallow minimum farther out. The deep chemisorption well measures the energy of adsorption.

choices.text: The bond dissociation energy of the molecule
choices.why: That is the energy to break the molecule apart in the gas phase. The well depth measures how strongly it binds to the surface.

explanation: The depth of the chemisorption well measures the strength of binding to the surface and is a direct representation of the energy of adsorption, ΔE(ads). The section notes that it is also often associated with the enthalpy of adsorption, ΔH(ads).

prompt: What does the position of the global minimum of the potential energy curve along the horizontal (d) axis give?

choices.text: The equilibrium bond distance d_ch
The energy of adsorption ΔE(ads)
choices.why: ΔE(ads) is the depth of the well, read on the energy axis. Its position on the d axis gives the equilibrium bond distance.

choices.text: The physisorption distance d_ph
choices.why: d_ph is the shallow physisorption minimum, farther out. The global minimum is the bottom of the chemisorption well, at d_ch.

choices.text: The point where the two curves cross
choices.why: The crossing lies farther out, where chemisorption begins to dominate. The global minimum is at the bond distance d_ch.

explanation: The global minimum is the bottom of the chemisorption well. Its location on the horizontal axis is d_ch, the equilibrium bond distance of the adsorbed molecule on this surface, while its depth is the energy of adsorption.

prompt: What sign does the section give the energy of adsorption, ΔE(ads), and why?

choices.text: Negative: the energy falls into the well
Positive: energy is needed for binding
choices.why: Binding releases energy; the molecule drops into a well. ΔE(ads), the energy change upon adsorption, is negative.

choices.text: Positive: it equals the heat of adsorption
choices.why: The heat of adsorption Q is the positive quantity, equal in size to −ΔH(ads). The energy of adsorption itself is negative.

choices.text: Zero, since there is no barrier
choices.why: That confuses ΔE(ads) with the activation energy of adsorption. With no barrier E_a^(ads) = 0, but the energy still falls by the well depth.

explanation: ΔE(ads) is the energy change upon adsorption, from a molecule far away to one at the bottom of the chemisorption well. The system's energy falls, so ΔE(ads) is negative, and its size is the depth of the well.

prompt: The section defines the heat of adsorption as Q = −ΔH(ads). If ΔH(ads) = −62 kJ mol^−1, what is Q, in kJ mol^−1?
explanation: Q = −ΔH(ads) = −(−62 kJ mol^−1) = 62 kJ mol^−1. The heat of adsorption is taken as a positive quantity, equal in magnitude to the (negative) enthalpy of adsorption.

prompt: For molecular chemisorption, the section's overall potential energy curve falls from the gas phase into the chemisorption well without ever rising above the starting energy. What is the activation energy for adsorption, E_a^(ads)?

choices.text: Zero
−ΔE(ads), the depth of the well
choices.why: The well depth is the barrier to desorption, climbing out. Going in, nothing has to be climbed, so E_a^(ads) = 0.

choices.text: The depth of the physisorption well
choices.why: Entering the physisorption well is downhill too, not a barrier. Nowhere is the curve above the starting energy, so E_a^(ads) = 0.

choices.text: The energy needed to break the molecule's bond
choices.why: In molecular chemisorption the molecule bonds to the surface whole, without dissociating. With no hump on the curve, E_a^(ads) = 0.

explanation: With no barrier to overcome on the way in, there is no activation energy of adsorption: E_a^(ads) = 0. The section adds the caution that this rests on the simple 1D model, which neglects orientation and other parameters.

prompt: For molecular chemisorption with no barrier to adsorption, which relation does the section give between the activation energy for desorption and the energy of adsorption?

choices.text: E_a^(des) = −ΔE(ads)
E_a^(des) = ΔE(ads)
choices.why: ΔE(ads) is negative, so this would make the barrier negative. The magnitudes are equal, so E_a^(des) = −ΔE(ads).

choices.text: E_a^(des) = 0
choices.why: It is adsorption that has no barrier. Desorption must climb out of the whole well, a significant barrier equal to −ΔE(ads).

choices.text: E_a^(des) < −ΔE(ads)
choices.why: With no hump on the curve, the molecule must climb the full depth of the well back to zero energy. The barrier equals −ΔE(ads).

explanation: To desorb, the molecule must climb from the bottom of the chemisorption well back up to the energy of the free molecule, the full depth of the well. Since ΔE(ads) is negative, E_a^(des) = −ΔE(ads), or approximately −ΔH(ads).

prompt: A molecule chemisorbs without dissociating and with no barrier to adsorption, and its activation energy for desorption is E_a^(des) = 118 kJ mol^−1. Using E_a^(des) = −ΔE(ads), what is ΔE(ads), in kJ mol^−1? (Include the sign.)
explanation: ΔE(ads) = −E_a^(des) = −118 kJ mol^−1. The barrier to desorption equals the full depth of the chemisorption well, and the energy of adsorption is negative because the system falls into that well.

prompt: An H_2 molecule far from a surface could first split into two H atoms, which then each bond to the surface. Why does the section call this route to dissociative chemisorption impractical?

choices.text: Breaking the H–H bond first costs about 435 kJ mol^−1
Free H atoms cannot form bonds to the surface
choices.why: They can: the H + H curve falls to a deep minimum, 2(M–H), with both atoms bonded. The trouble is the energy needed to split H_2 first.

choices.text: The H–H bond is too weak to be worth breaking
choices.why: It is the reverse: the H–H bond dissociation energy is large, about 435 kJ mol^−1 or 4.5 eV. That down payment is the problem.

choices.text: Splitting H_2 releases more energy than the surface takes up
choices.why: Splitting H_2 absorbs energy rather than releasing it. That required input, D_(H-H) ≈ 435 kJ mol^−1, is what makes the route impractical.

explanation: Far from the surface, two separate H atoms lie D_(H-H) ≈ 435 kJ mol^−1 (4.5 eV) above an H_2 molecule. The section calls this energy down payment far too severe, so instead the molecule approaches along the physisorption curve.

prompt: In Figure 31.6.10, the H + H curve starts far from the surface and falls to a minimum labeled 2(M–H). What does that minimum represent?

choices.text: Two H atoms, each bonded to the surface
Two free H atoms far from the surface
choices.why: Those are at the start of the H + H curve, lying D_(H-H) above H_2. The minimum is where both atoms have formed bonds to the surface.

choices.text: An H_2 molecule physisorbed on the surface
choices.why: Physisorbed H_2 sits in the shallow well of the separate physisorption curve. 2(M–H) is the minimum of the chemisorption curve for two H atoms.

choices.text: An H_2 molecule chemisorbed in one piece
choices.why: That would be molecular chemisorption. Here the molecule is dissociated, and each H atom is bonded to the surface, M.

explanation: The H + H curve is the chemisorption curve for two separated H atoms. As they approach, both can form strong bonds to the substrate, and the minimum 2(M–H) is that dissociatively chemisorbed state.

prompt: Take an H_2 molecule far from the surface as zero energy; two separate H atoms far from the surface then lie D_(H-H) = 435 kJ mol^−1 higher. If the 2(M–H) minimum lies 525 kJ mol^−1 below the energy of the two free H atoms, what is its energy relative to gas-phase H_2, in kJ mol^−1? (Include the sign.)
explanation: The 2(M–H) state lies at 435 kJ mol^−1 − 525 kJ mol^−1 = −90 kJ mol^−1. Dissociative chemisorption of H_2 is downhill overall, even though reaching it by first breaking the H–H bond would need a 435 kJ mol^−1 down payment.

prompt: An H_2 molecule approaches the surface along the physisorption curve with enough energy to pass straight into the dissociative chemisorption well, without being held in the physisorption well. What does the section call this?

choices.text: Direct chemisorption
Precursor-mediated chemisorption
choices.why: That route has the molecule held first in a transient physisorbed state. Passing straight into the chemisorption well is direct chemisorption.

choices.text: Molecular chemisorption
choices.why: In molecular chemisorption the molecule stays whole. Here H_2 ends up dissociated, and it gets there directly.

choices.text: Physisorption
choices.why: The molecule doesn't stop in the physisorption well; it ends in the chemisorption well, bonded as two H atoms.

explanation: A hydrogen molecule first approaches along the physisorption curve. If it has sufficient energy, it can pass straight into the chemisorption well, which the section calls direct chemisorption.

prompt: In precursor-mediated chemisorption of H_2, what is the precursor?

choices.text: The transiently physisorbed H_2 molecule
Two free H atoms far from the surface
choices.why: Reaching that state needs the 435 kJ mol^−1 down payment, which is not practical. The precursor is H_2 held briefly in the physisorption well.

choices.text: The chemisorbed 2(M–H) state
choices.why: 2(M–H) is where the process ends, not the state leading to it. The precursor is the transiently physisorbed molecule.

choices.text: The crossing point of the two curves
choices.why: The crossing is the barrier the molecule passes over, not a state that holds it. The precursor is the physisorbed molecule before it crosses.

explanation: In this route the molecule first undergoes transient physisorption and then crosses into the dissociated, chemisorbed state. The physisorbed molecule is the precursor, which is why the section calls it precursor-mediated chemisorption.

prompt: An H_2 molecule is held transiently in the physisorption well, on the way to dissociative chemisorption. According to the section, what can it do next?

choices.text: Desorb as a molecule, or cross into the chemisorbed state
Only cross into the chemisorbed state
choices.why: Being physisorbed doesn't commit the molecule. It can also desorb back into the gas phase as a molecule.

choices.text: Desorb as two H atoms, or cross into the chemisorbed state
choices.why: The physisorbed molecule is still intact H_2, so it desorbs as a molecule. It dissociates only by crossing into the chemisorbed state.

choices.text: Dissociate in the physisorption well and stay there
choices.why: The physisorption well holds the intact molecule. Dissociation happens by crossing the barrier into the chemisorption well.

explanation: From the transient physisorbed state, the molecule can either desorb back into the gas phase as a molecule or cross over the barrier into the dissociated, chemisorbed state. Taking the second path is precursor-mediated chemisorption.

prompt: According to the section, what decides whether the dissociative adsorption of a molecule is activated or non-activated?

choices.text: Where the two curves cross, relative to zero energy
How deep the physisorption well is
choices.why: H_2's physisorption well is very small, yet that doesn't change the conclusion. The location of the curve crossing decides whether there is a barrier.

choices.text: How deep the chemisorption well is
choices.why: The well depth gives the energy of adsorption, not the barrier on the way in. The barrier is set by where the curves cross.

choices.text: Whether the molecule chemisorbs directly or via a precursor
choices.why: Both routes pass over the same curve crossing. Whether it lies above or below zero energy decides whether adsorption is activated.

explanation: If the crossing of the molecular physisorption curve and the dissociative chemisorption curve lies below the initial zero energy, there is no barrier. If it lies above, there is an activation barrier to chemisorption, which has a major influence on the kinetics of adsorption.

prompt: For a dissociative adsorption, the curve crossing lies just below zero energy, so adsorption is non-activated. A small shift of the chemisorption curve moves the crossing to just above zero. What happens?

choices.text: Adsorption becomes activated, with a barrier
Nothing much; small shifts barely matter
choices.why: The section warns that relatively small shifts in either curve can significantly alter the size of any barrier. Here one appears.

choices.text: Desorption loses its barrier
choices.why: Desorption still has to climb out of the chemisorption well. It is the way in that now meets a barrier at the crossing.

choices.text: The physisorption well disappears
choices.why: Only the chemisorption curve moved; the physisorption well is unchanged. What changes is the height of the crossing, which is now a barrier.

explanation: The barrier to dissociative chemisorption is set by the crossing point of the two curves. Once the crossing lies above the initial zero energy, the molecule must climb to it, so adsorption is activated, and that barrier has a major influence on the kinetics of adsorption.

prompt: The section notes that the physisorption well of H_2 is very small, in some cases negligible. How does this affect its conclusions about dissociative adsorption?

choices.text: They still hold: it may be activated or not
Dissociative adsorption of H_2 is always activated
choices.why: The shallow well doesn't settle this. Whether there is a barrier still depends on where the curves cross.

choices.text: Dissociative adsorption of H_2 is never activated
choices.why: A small physisorption well doesn't remove a barrier at the crossing. The process may be activated or not, depending on the crossing.

choices.text: The model no longer applies to H_2
choices.why: The section says the small well does not alter the basic conclusions. The model still applies, with the crossing deciding the barrier.

explanation: A shallow physisorption well does not alter the basic conclusion of the model: dissociative adsorption may be either activated or non-activated depending on the exact location of the curve crossing. For other molecules the physisorption well is deeper.

prompt: On a potential energy curve for dissociative adsorption, the free molecule is at zero energy, the curve crossing lies at +20 kJ mol^−1, and the bottom of the chemisorption well lies at −105 kJ mol^−1. What is the activation energy for desorption, E_a^(des), in kJ mol^−1?
explanation: To desorb, the adsorbed molecule climbs from the well bottom to the top of the barrier: E_a^(des) = 20 − (−105) = 125 kJ mol^−1. That is larger than −ΔE(ads) = 105 kJ mol^−1 by the barrier to adsorption, E_a^(ads) = 20 kJ mol^−1.

prompt: For an activated dissociative adsorption, the section gives E_a^(des) − E_a^(ads) = −ΔE(ads). If E_a^(ads) = 35 kJ mol^−1 and E_a^(des) = 180 kJ mol^−1, what is ΔE(ads), in kJ mol^−1? (Include the sign.)
explanation: −ΔE(ads) = 180 − 35 = 145 kJ mol^−1, so ΔE(ads) = −145 kJ mol^−1. Equating E_a^(des) with −ΔE(ads) here would overstate the well depth by the 35 kJ mol^−1 barrier to adsorption.

prompt: Even when adsorption has a barrier, the section says E_a^(des) ≈ −ΔH(ads) is still commonly used. Why is this approximation reasonable?

choices.text: E_a^(ads) is nearly always much smaller than E_a^(des)
E_a^(ads) is always exactly zero
choices.why: With a barrier, E_a^(ads) is not zero. It is just usually very much smaller than E_a^(des), so dropping it changes little.

choices.text: E_a^(des) is nearly always much smaller than E_a^(ads)
choices.why: It is the other way round. The barrier to adsorption is usually the small one, so E_a^(des) ≈ −ΔE(ads).

choices.text: Desorption has no barrier when adsorption does
choices.why: Desorption has to climb out of the chemisorption well and over the barrier, so its barrier is the larger one.

explanation: The exact relation is E_a^(des) − E_a^(ads) = −ΔE(ads). Because E_a^(ads) is nearly always very much smaller than E_a^(des), and the energy and enthalpy of adsorption differ very little, E_a^(des) ≈ −ΔH(ads) is still a good approximation.

prompt: An adsorption has E_a^(ads) = 6 kJ mol^−1 and E_a^(des) = 150 kJ mol^−1. The exact relation is E_a^(des) − E_a^(ads) = −ΔE(ads). By what percentage does the approximation −ΔE(ads) ≈ E_a^(des) overstate the true −ΔE(ads)?
explanation: Exactly, −ΔE(ads) = 150 − 6 = 144 kJ mol^−1; the approximation gives 150 kJ mol^−1, which is (150 − 144)/144 × 100 = 4.17% too high. Because E_a^(ads) is usually much smaller than E_a^(des), the shortcut is only a few percent off.
